articles.title: Volunteers from Poland remember how Poles opened their homes to Ukrainian refugees in 2022
articles.author: Anna Romandash
paras: Now, Russian disinformation fuels the memory of violent historic conflicts, and Polish empathy is burning out
Originally published on Global Voices

Folkowisko during the “Borderland Memory” project, bringing Ukrainian and Polish youth together to preserve shared historical heritage, restore historic cemeteries, and strengthen cross-cultural friendship. Photo: Folkowisko. Used with permission.

Marcin Piotrowski remembers the beginning of his work in Ukraine through the Budomierz-Hruszów border crossing in February 2022, days after the launch of Russia’s war on Ukraine. “We crossed the border on the second day after the full-scale invasion,” he says, “and there were hundreds of people there. Nobody was helping them.”

People were waiting for days to enter Poland, some in cars and some on foot, as temperatures fell to around minus 15 degrees Celsius. On the Polish side, food and transport had been organised, but the queues on the Ukrainian side had become a challenge of their own. Piotrowski and volunteers from his Polish association, Folkowisko, decided to intervene. “We had experience because our association organises festivals,” he explains. “We put up tents, brought volunteers, and our medical service from the festival came as well. Later, we started helping at other border crossings, then in Lviv at the railway station, and we began working with volunteers from different parts of Ukraine.”

What began as emergency assistance developed into a network of projects across the Polish-Ukrainian border. Folkowisko helped establish a medical clinic and education centre in Nakhachiv, near the Polish border, where Polish and Ukrainian cultural workers have held joint workshops. The organisation has also supported psychological care, trained Ukrainian psychologists and social workers, and brought Ukrainian families affected by the war to Poland for temporary respite.

But Folkowisko's work is not only about the present. Piotrowski is also interested in the history of the border region, and in what happens when difficult memories are discussed through contact rather than isolation. “Before the Second World War, there were more than a thousand Ukrainians in the village where we work,” he says, referring to a locality in what is now eastern Poland. “Today, there are 43 people and they are all Polish. People were resettled in 1945 and 1947, during Operation Vistula. This was a place where Jews, Poles and Ukrainians lived together, and 80 years ago you could not really say where the border was.”

The history separating the two societies is particularly painful. During World War II, tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed by Ukrainian nationalist formations in the Volhynia region. Polish nationalist groups retaliated, killing thousands of Ukrainian civilians. The competing memories of these events have remained politically sensitive, especially in families whose relatives were victims.

After the fall of communism, the history of Volhynia became increasingly prominent in Polish public debate. In Ukraine, meanwhile, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) acquired an important place in national memory because of its role in the struggle for Ukrainian independence against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. Disputes over monuments, commemorations, exhumations and historical figures have repeatedly affected relations between Warsaw and Kyiv.

The subject is also vulnerable to manipulation, according to Łukasz Wojtkowski, an assistant professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, who researches information operations and disinformation. He argues that historical grievances can be connected to contemporary fears and used to deepen divisions: “Volhynia is a playbook for propaganda and disguised disinformation,” he explains. “It is basically the only open case between those two nations that can spark the engine of disinformation and hatred. Russia can put two irons in the fire at the same time: it can increase the hatred between Poland and Ukraine, and it can reinforce the Russian narrative that there is a fascist regime in Kyiv.”

Anna Mierzyńska, a Polish journalist and social media researcher specialising in disinformation, has studied similar narratives targeting Polish audiences. “Reliable historical debate,” she stresses, “is always based on listening to both sides and taking new developments into account. Its purpose is not to attack or create hatred, but to explain what happened and find an understanding.” While there is such a debate among historians and experts, she adds that in the Polish information sphere, “many of the posts on this subject are designed to provoke hatred toward Ukrainians.”

Recurring narratives portray Ukrainians as a physical threat to Poles, Mierzyńska continues, using descriptions of the Volhynia crimes to create fear, or to suggest that Ukrainians could seek Polish territory. Existing social problems can also be folded into the same narrative. Long waiting lists for healthcare, for example, existed before the arrival of millions of Ukrainian refugees, but online claims blamed Ukrainians for them. Housing, employment and public services have been framed in similar ways.

The scale of Ukrainian displacement makes the relationship especially important. In 2026, nearly a million Ukrainians took temporary protection in Poland, representing 21.8 percent of all people from Ukraine under temporary protection in the European Union.

We need good contacts between Poles and Ukrainians, integration, getting to know each other and building trust. When we know each other well and trust each other, outside influence becomes much less important. – Anna Mierzyńska

For Piotrowski, the first months after the invasion demonstrated what such contact can look like. “Ordinary citizens living on the border with Ukraine were the first ones to provide immediate support,” he recalls. “I have never seen so much kindness in my life on both sides of the border, and so much reconciliation and understanding.”

Five years into the full-scale war, however, the border has also revealed the limits of that extraordinary solidarity. “I understand that when Poles opened their homes, it could become difficult,” Piotrowski says. “Someone comes who speaks another language, has slightly different customs and wants to stay for a long time. This is what I call empathy burnout.”

He does not regard that exhaustion as proof that the solidarity of 2022 was false, but rather, as a relationship being tested by time. His response is the same one that drives Folkowisko’s cultural work: more contact. “Poles don't know Ukrainians, Ukrainians don't know Poles,” he says. “Our job is to make people meet each other and understand each other.”

This approach means bringing difficult history into conversations in much the same way that Folkowisko’s festivals and programmes bring Polish and Ukrainian participants together while addressing the violence and displacement that transformed the region.

Wojtkowski is more cautious about whether historical reconciliation alone could resolve the wider conflict over competing narratives. “Imagine that tomorrow Poland and Ukraine commemorate every victim, Ukraine admits who was killed and how many people died, Poland admits what happened on its side, and all the exhumations are completed,” he posits. “It would not change everything, because Russia has other narratives.”

He maintains that, when it comes to history, both Polish and Ukrainian society did not do their homework properly. “In Poland, we learned the story of the interwar period as the restoration of the Polish state after more than a hundred years without independence,” he says, “but we did not always learn enough about the Ukrainian experience within that state. Ukraine has its own work to do in confronting everything that happened during the Second World War.”

Wojtkowski further advises that both Poland and Ukraine “should step very carefully, as if on very thin ice.” According to him, there should be signs of goodwill and a willingness to cooperate, but there is still a lot to do politically, academically and socially.

For Piotrowski, however, governments and historians do not have to resolve everything before ordinary people can build relationships: “We are trying to connect people who live ten or 15 kilometres from each other. They have different memories, different histories, but they can still meet and work together.”

As Ukraine moves toward the European Union, and as Polish and Ukrainian lives become increasingly intertwined, those everyday relationships may shape how the two societies handle their shared past. “If we lose the contact between ordinary people across both countries,” Piotrowski maintains, “then it becomes much easier to build the walls. And once the walls are there, it is much harder to build the bridges again.”
You can listen to an audio version of this story here.
Nata Yasevych is a multimedia producer, media maker, and journalist, covering social issues and politics.

articles.title: Vote young yet govern much later: West African youth’s struggle for power
articles.author: Laura
paras: In all of West Africa, te voting age is 18, but presidential eligibility ages vary widely
Originally published on Global Voices
Youth mobilized in Africa. Screenshot from DW Africa's YouTube channel

In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18. In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25. However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50 years old before being eligible to run for the highest office. Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.

Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them. They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves. The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?

Across the region, the voting age is 18. However, presidential eligibility ages vary widely. In Gambia, it’s 30; in Senegal, Nigeria, and Côte d’Ivoire, it’s 35; and in Benin, Ghana, and Guinea, it’s 40. In the legislative assemblies, the bar is even lower. In Togo, Benin, Senegal, and Nigeria’s House of Representatives, it’s 25, while in Ghana it’s 21.

The situation in Togo requires closer inspection. On May 6, 2024, the country legally became a parliamentary republic. Under the 2024 Constitution, the eligibility age for President of the Republic is 50. Parliament also now elects the president, whose powers are limited. Authority now rests with the President of the Council of Ministers, who must be at least 40 and is not elected in public presidential elections. Faure Gnassingbé has held this position since May 3, 2025, the day parliament also elected the country’s oldest-ever incoming president of the Republic, Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, 86.
However, the country’s legal age limit is hardly set in stone. In 2002, the National Assembly lowered it from 45 to 35 — a reform the opposition called tailor-made for Faure Gnassingbé.

More recently, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, on July 30, 2026, the Ghanaian government agreed in principle to lower the minimum presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35, defying the Constitutional Review Committee’s recommendation of 30. This legislation will ultimately go to a referendum, requiring a 40 percent turnout and a 75 percent approval.

In 2018, Nigeria set a regional precedent. Under pressure from the youth-led Not Too Young To Run campaign, the law lowered the presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35 and the House of Representatives’ eligibility age from 30 to 25.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union, lowering the minimum presidential age leads to younger parliaments. However, Côte d’Ivoire tells a very different story. In 2016, after removing the maximum age limit of 75 to run for office, incumbent President Alassane Ouattara, 83, ran for another term in 2025. The law rarely protects younger generations.
Youths particularly active in street movements

Even though young people have the right to vote across the continent, that does not mean all young people exercise that right. In August 2025, an Afrobarometer survey found that those aged 18 to 35 were less active than their elders in almost all traditional means of political participation. Overall across the continent, they trailed by 18 percentage points in voting, but by a record 29 points in Senegal. Protests were the only exception.

In Togo’s capital of Lomé, the June 6 Movement, sparked by the rapper Aamron’s arrest, brought thousands of people onto the streets. According to the Media Foundation for West Africa, the subsequent crackdown, for which the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) blamed government-backed militiamen, left seven dead.

Similarly, in Madagascar, the September 2025 protests toppled President Andry Rajoelina’s government, resulting in a military takeover. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the overthrown president himself came to power in 2019 on the back of a protest, at just 34 years old.

Comparably, in Kenya, street protests forced the withdrawal of the 2024 Finance Bill. Meanwhile, in Morocco, youth-led protests prompted the authorities to announce youth candidacy incentives and prosecute specific ringleaders.
Although leaderless movements wrest concessions, they rarely last without political parties or trade unions to sustain them.
The gap between participation and representation

The Inter-Parliamentary Report, published on April 9, 2026, found that elected officials aged 30 and under account for just 2.8 percent of all parliamentarians worldwide. Since 2023, progress has stalled for the first time since 2014. More than a third (37.1 percent) of legislative houses have no parliamentarians in this age group.

The lack of youth representation and participation is a significant challenge considering young people under 35 account for roughly 70 percent of West Africa’s population, according to the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), at the start of Ghana’s 2025 parliamentary term, despite the legal minimum age of 21, no parliamentarians were aged 30 or under. What’s more, those aged 31 to 40 held just 46 of the 269 parliamentary seats, or 17.1 percent. After Senegal’s 2024 legislative elections, the National Assembly had only five members under 30, accounting for just 3 percent. Although almost 38 percent of registered voters were aged 18 to 35, the Assembly’s average age was 47. Elected at just 44, the country’s youngest-ever president, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, only became an official candidate after his mentor, Ousmane Sonko, was disqualified.

In Nigeria, International IDEA, an intergovernmental organization that supports sustainable democracy worldwide, reported that in 2015, only three of the 360 members of the House of Representatives were between the ages of 18–25, rising to 14 in 2019 — a positive but modest development.
In Dakar, the head of Yiaga Africa, the organization behind the Not Too Young to Run campaign, summed up the situation, stating that the political arena is more open on paper than in reality.

However, Afrobarometer has identified a paradox. While young people do vote less than their elders, they are also excluded from seats of power and the polls. This representation gap is anything but passive; it breeds disengagement. The IPU warns that young people’s absence from parliamentary assemblies undermines institutional legitimacy and jeopardizes trust in democracy. Senegal, listed in the 2026 IPU report as one of the countries where parliament grew younger in the most recent elections, shows that rejuvenation is possible when a political agenda empowers a generation.
Rewriting the deal: money, parties, obstacles

High age limit proponents demand experience. Across the 34 countries that Afrobarometer surveyed, citizens favor an average leadership age of 39. Those calling for a lower age limit seek proven engagement measures, such as lowering the eligibility age, quotas, and forums for young parliamentarians. However, as Nigeria shows, often, the main obstacle is financial.

Nigeria’s ruling party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), has set the total cost of its 2027 presidential nomination and expression-of-interest forms at NGN 100 million (USD 75,000), NGN 30 million (USD 22,521) for the expression of interest, and NGN 70 million (USD 52,550) for the nomination. The Senate will cost NGN 20 million (USD 15,014) and the House of Representatives NGN 10 million (USD 7,507).

Young people will receive a 50 percent discount only on nomination fees, leaving the presidential bill at NGN 65 million (USD 48,789). A Nigerian civil society group calculated that workers earning the minimum wage, NGN 70,000 (USD 52) per month, would have to work for more than a century to buy some of these forms.

The Electoral Act, 2026, signed on February 18, also doubled the presidential candidate’s campaign spending limit to NGN 10 billion (USD 7.5 million) and tripled that of governorship candidates to NGN 3 billion (USD 2.2 million).

At the initiative of ECOWAS and the youth-led advocacy organization Legis360, delegates from 12 countries gathered in Dakar to bring these obstacles to the forefront. In their communiqué, they launched the West Africa Youth Observer Network (WAYON) and called for youth quotas, reduced candidate fees, and spending limits. ECOWAS later announced it would deploy youth-only election observers for Nigeria’s upcoming presidential election on January 16, 2027.

Other countries exemplify how laws can directly impact nominations. According to the IPU, Ecuador owes much of its progress to a 2022 law, which required 25 percent of its candidates to be young adults. Countries with term limits also have considerably more young parliamentarians than the global average. In 2023, the IPU also noted that limited youth funding and a lack of spending limits contributed to aging parliamentary assemblies.

Elsewhere, the obstacles are political. Take, for example, Benin. After disqualifying the main opposition candidate (Les Démocrates) for failing to meet election requirements, current President Romuald Wadagni faced only one opponent (Paul Hounkpe). On April 12, 2026, Wadagni subsequently won the presidential election with 94.27 percent of the vote. In 2024, a constitutional reform that extended the presidential term from five to seven years also raised the minimum vote threshold for securing seats in the National Assembly from 10 percent of parliamentary election votes to 20 percent. This regulation far outweighs a candidate’s date of birth when they have no party machine behind them.

Another example is Burkina Faso. In January 2026, the military junta dissolved all political parties. Meanwhile, in The Gambia, President Barrow will run for a third term in the December 5 presidential election.
Inclusive voting, but flawed representation

Is a system that gives young people the right to elect their leader but impedes their ability to become one themselves fully inclusive? The findings speak for themselves. Although Nigeria has lowered its age limits and Ghana has committed to doing the same, these limits are more a symptom than a cause. Age is not the sole contributing factor.

Critics argue that lowering age limits without also addressing nomination costs, party regulations, and the openness of the political arena would only be the first step on a seemingly endless staircase. What stands between young people and decision-making positions are exceedingly high costs, restrictive nomination practices, candidate exclusions, and even the lack of parties.

Until street movements have credible institutional representatives, they will continue to wrest temporary concessions or, as seen in Madagascar, give way to powers other than those they had hoped for. The primary challenge of the West African Democratic Pact is making young people not only the promised future of politics, but also an active part of today’s representation.

articles.title: In opting for Lula, Brazil made a conservative choice to elect a man of the left over one of the far right
articles.author: João Gabriel de Lima, Jornalista, doutorando em Política Comparada, Universidade de Lisboa
paras: The 2026 elections in Brazil played out amid an widespread assumption repeated around the world: that the country was polarized and that would inform the vote.

But the word “polarization” implies symmetry – and symmetry is something that never existed in the contest between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. On one side, a moderate center-left politician with a center-right running mate, Geraldo Alckmin. On the other, a representative of the radical right and a member of an international movement that critics say threatens democracies around the world.

Flávio is no mere conservative. While he may be courted and supported by the members of the Republican Party in the U.S., his policies put him more in the mold of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany and Portugal’s Enough, a party that advocates the repatriation of immigrants and a ban on Muslim places of worship.

On the day he launched his candidacy, at an event of Brazil’s Liberal Party (PL) in São Paulo, Flávio laid out three of the guiding principles of what his administration would look like. First was the so called “Project Darkness”, a crime-fighting plan inspired by by El Salvador’s hard-right President Nayib Bukele. Second was joining the Shield of the Americas, U.S. President Donald Trump’s military and political initiative for the continent. Thirdly, Flávio laid out plans for the “tesouraço” or “big cut” – a slashing of public spending modeled after Argentinian President Javier Milei’s “chainsaw” economic policy. Since he didn’t provide any details, it’s unclear whether it would be just as sharp as Milei’s, but it was enough to strike fear into those who depend on social programs to survive.

Milei himself was at the launch event. He arrived singing the song The Panic Show by the Argentine hard rock band La Renga. Flávio accompanied Milei in the song’s refrain: “Yo soy el león, soy el rey y te destrozaré” (“I am the lion, I am the king, and I will tear you apart”) while dancing along with the Argentine president.

It is, I believe, the form, more than the content, that defines the members of the far-right brotherhood that threatens democracies around the world. They are politicians who do not like to negotiate, even though negotiation is the essence of politics. They want to annihilate the “enemy”, as if they were, literally, on a battlefield.

Flávio’s ideas are clearly “misplaced ideas,” to borrow the term coined by Brazilian literary critic, essayist, and professor Roberto Schwarz. It is impossible to implement Nayib Bukele’s crime-fighting plan — which allows for the arrest of any citizen without a formal charge, the right for legal counsel, or habeas corpus — in a democratic country.

On the economy side, in the midst of a debt crisis, Brazil does needs a fiscal adjustment. However, the country’s economic situation bears no resemblance to that of Argentina, a country that has seen its currency collapse and is rolling over dollar denominated debt.

A recent report in the Financial Times portrayed what is known in Brazil as Bolsonarism as a clan similar to the Roy family from the American television series “Succession.” Nothing could be more apt. Flávio is not Flávio. He is merely a generic offshoot of the Bolsonaro brand. During the Brazilian TV Globo election debate held right before the runoff of last Sunday, Oct. 25, he referred to his now jailed father administration as “our government.” If he were elected president, Flávio would have governed under Jair’s supervision and alongside his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro - a former congressman now living in the U.S. to escape a arrest warrant - who serves as the point of contact between Bolsonarism and the radical and far right around the world.

Eduardo is close to former Hungary prime minister Viktor Orbán, Spain’s Santiago Abascal, president of Spanish far-right party Vox, El Salvador’s Bukele, France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen, and the most radical wing of the U.S. Republican Party.

Flávio spent the election campaign trying to pretend he wasn’t like his father. He marketed himself as the “moderate Bolsonaro.” But Bolsonarism, in Brazilian politics, is synonymous with extremism. The mask slipped during his final speech. If he were a democrat, he would have conceded the indisputable defeat suffered on Oct. 25. Instead, he refused to concede and vowed to challenge the results.

But how did Lula defeat Flávio? My hypothesis is that Brazilians made a conservative choice. Lula has already governed the country three times. Voters know what to expect from him. His opponent, on the other hand, is seen widely as the Brazilian member of a radical global right wing movement, and whose leader is in prison for attempting a coup. The images of vandals destroying the buildings that house the federal executive, legislative, and judicial branches of Brazil’s government on 8 Jan. 2023 – an echo of the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol riot in the U.S. – are still vivid in the memory of Brazilians.
Faced with a choice between something they already know and the unpredictability of extremists, Brazilians opted for the conservative vote. Being prudent, they did not want to risk their democracy.

articles.title: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power
articles.author: Gavin Brent Sullivan, Professor of Social Psychology, International Psychoanalytic University Berlin
paras: Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.

The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across Serbian society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and creeping authoritarianism of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.

In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the Pledge EU Horizon project. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.

The protesters’ grievances were centred on the 2024 collapse of a roof at the newly renovated Novi Sad train station in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. Allegations of state involvement through corruption in the procurement process and lowered building standards have been denied by the government. But they nonetheless sparked large nationwide protests.

Focus group participants expressed anger and underlying fear about harassment during the protests by what they said were government-funded gangs. They also spoke of their concern at the threats and violence directed towards them, not only as they protested but also when walking in areas near government buildings in main cities. Several students reported feeling threatened even in their own homes.

At the same time, the students voiced dissatisfaction with teachers who were not supportive of their movement, and other students who opposed them. This dissatisfaction extended to older family members and relatives who repeated government-controlled media fabrications about the protests. These included claims that the students were being paid by foreign anti-Serbian groups.

Despite the fear of arrest or worse, and despondency that change could really occur, the students who took part in the focus groups were resilient. They were focused on their long-term goal of regime change, with many students talking with pride about creating a leaderless movement that was organising candidates to challenge Vučić in an election.

Several participants reported feeling spontaneous, intense experiences of national pride when taking part in the protests. Some spoke of taking back national symbols such as the Serbian flag to counter propaganda that they were not patriotic and wanted to destroy the country.
Feelings of solidarity were also experienced when minority Bosniak Muslim students from Novi Pazar University in south-western Serbia joined the protests. As one participant said:

They’re a minority which was at odds with Serbia, with Serbian nationals actually. So now we had that part of reunification with them and they’re a Muslim minority. They are really active in these protests and student protests and it’s been wonderful.

Another member of the focus group noted that they expected elections to be “brutal”. But they were optimistic about the prospect of unseating the Vučić government. They said: “I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.”

At the same time, most of the students did not dare to dream that they would succeed in ousting a government that had held a 12-year grip on power. It is stunning now after Vučić’s concession speech in which he admitted “it is clear that we have lost these elections” to know that they were successful just one year later.

The remarkable victory of the Student List should give hope to any group opposing a corrupt, authoritarian regime that a core commitment to democracy is precisely what attracts voters to choose progressive change.

However, while there will be euphoria, pride and tears of joy in Serbia as the election result sinks in, there may also be groups who are fearful of change and that the new government may seek accountability for members of the ousted regime. Some theorists of political emotions talk about the possibility for revenge to be enacted by winners, especially when a fight for power has been bitter.

For those on the losing side, meanwhile, electoral defeat can bring grief, anxiety and anger. But acknowledging these emotions and coming to terms with loss can bring openness to change. In his concession speech, Vučić said: “I do not want unrest, I do not want killings, I do not want anything like that on the streets.”

The Student List’s commitment to democracy, pluralism and justice should also override any desire for redress. The movement has actively avoided developing a victim identity, taking responsibility for enacting change themselves.
As one focus group participant said:

Of course, they [the government] are the problem. I’m not trying to deny that. But I would blame us more … because, I mean, we chose them, we keep choosing them. Okay, they do steal when it comes to the elections, they do many things, they hide, they try to control the media and everything. But at the same time, we don’t have the opposition and we have that state of mind that is allowing them to do everything they’re doing.

There are various other challenges facing the Student List. These include adapting the movement’s leaderless organisational assemblage into a government capable of delivering the reforms required for EU membership.

But regardless of what happens next, it was certainly a privilege to talk to the students at a time when change did not seem possible and to provide encouragement and support when there was little outside recognition of their struggles and sacrifices.

articles.title: Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track
articles.author: Guilherme Casarões, Associate Professor of Brazilian Studies, Florida International University
paras: Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.
At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.
On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.
The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.
Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.

Second, no Brazilian president has ever been elected to four terms. When his new term ends, Lula will have governed Brazil for 16 (non-consecutive) years – the longest democratically elected tenure in the country’s history.

Only Getúlio Vargas governed longer. He held power for almost two decades through a revolution, dictatorship and democratic election from the 1930–50s, and is widely considered Brazil’s most consequential president.
Third, no runoff campaign in Brazil has ever brought so many people to the streets and onto social media, supporting both sides.
Unlike the first round, the second round was not quiet, nor was it decided by television ads. Brazil saw a mass mobilization of voters, and it was ferocious.
The Brazilian left fought an uphill battle against social media platforms, economic elites, and a Supreme Electoral Court whose president was accused of trying to tip the balance to favour Bolsonaro.
Lula has a long record of political miracles, and he has added another one to the list.
An election result that matters beyond Brazil
Lula’s victory matters well beyond Brazil’s borders, also in three ways.
Globally, Brazil remains a bulwark against the rise of the far right. In recent elections across Latin America and Europe, far-right parties and leaders have advanced almost everywhere.
Brazil, the world’s fourth-largest democracy, has now bucked the trend, and is a symbol that democrats elsewhere will not ignore.

Regionally, Lula has defied the so-called “incumbent curse”. Over the past decade in Latin America, governing parties have lost election after election, punished by voters for inflation, insecurity and economic stagnation.
Brazil’s economy was in reasonable shape, but its gains were modest and unevenly felt. Everything pointed to a defeat, and Lula beat the odds anyway.

His win is also a check on what critics have called the “Donroe Doctrine”, referring to the Trump administration’s push to bring the Western Hemisphere more firmly into the US sphere of influence through tariffs, threats and political patronage.
Bolsonaro had campaigned as Washington’s preferred partner in South America. Brazil’s voters turned that offer down.

Domestically, the result also shows the power of popular mobilisation on the left. After Lula’s poor first-round showing, Lula’s campaign re-energised demoralised supporters and built a broad coalition of voters, some of whom were voting less for Lula than against what Bolsonaro represents. It also mobilised people who had stayed home in the first round to get out to vote.

Lula should not mistake survival for vindication. Yes, he corrected course. In three weeks, he acknowledged the mistakes he made over four years in office, especially during a lacklustre first-round campaign. He sharpened his message, widened his alliances and spoke directly to the voters he had lost. That is no small achievement for a politician, however experienced he may be.
But he now has to govern a country more polarised than ever. Political violence on the streets has increased, and hate speech circulates freely online.

Prominent figures on the far right, including Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, have already said they will not accept this election result. Bolsonaro said late Sunday he will not concede, and will seek an annulment of the vote.

And then there is Washington. Given the White House’s close ties to the Bolsonaro family, there is a real risk the Trump administration will question, or even refuse to recognise, the outcome of the election. That would be extraordinary, and a few years ago, it would have been unthinkable.

Things are further complicated by a legal battle on election day itself. After allegations of voter suppression of Lula’s supporters in several cities, the justices of Brazil’s Supreme Court and Supreme Electoral Court clashed over whether to extend voting hours. Whatever the legal merits, the dispute gives the losing side a ready-made narrative of “voting irregularities”.
This could be a matter of serious concern, and it may last for weeks.
Three questions for Lula’s next term
When Lula is inaugurated on January 5, three questions will define his fourth term.
The first is how Lula will govern a deeply divided country with a conservative majority in Congress and over a dozen right-wing state governors.

The legislature that held him hostage over the past four years has grown more hostile, not less. Every budget, every reform and every appointment will be a tough negotiation, with the possibility of an impeachment hanging over Lula’s head.
The second is repair. How will he deal with problems that go well beyond partisan disputes?
These include fiscal pressures from rising government spending, a steady loss of trust in democratic institutions, and an institutional system that no longer works as designed.

The Supreme Court, once the guarantor of the democratic order, has seen its legitimacy eroded by a major financial scandal surrounding Banco Master. Although the president cannot “repair” a court, he can refuse to treat the crisis as someone else’s problem.
The third question is the most important. Will Lula, his Workers’ Party (PT) and Brazil’s broader democratic forces use this reprieve to renew Brazilian politics? That would mean:
new political leadership alternatives beyond the ageing leaders who have dominated the left for 40 years
new forms of popular political participation that do not depend on a single charismatic figure
a new narrative that speaks to the precarious workers, religious families and angry voters who have drifted toward the far right.
This is the only real antidote to polarisation, and it will not come from a single election or a single leader.
Lula’s comeback has bought Brazil time. Whether it buys anything more depends on what he and his allies do over the next four years, one step at a time.
Lula has worked another miracle. His last task is to make sure Brazil does not need another one.

Guilherme Casarões não presta consultoria, trabalha, possui ações ou recebe financiamento de qualquer empresa ou organização que poderia se beneficiar com a publicação deste artigo e não revelou nenhum vínculo relevante além de seu cargo acadêmico.

articles.title: Between two shores: The ‘Monhés,’ nationality, and a sense of belonging in Mozambique
articles.author: Liam Anderson
paras: Being Mozambican is a matter of belonging — regardless of one’s origin, appearance, or surname
Originally published on Global Voices
Indians in Mozambique celebrating the Hindu festival of Navratri. Image by Kash_if via Flickr. CC BY 2.0.

In Mozambique, the word monhé has a much deeper history than its everyday use might suggest. Depending on who says it and the context, it can simply be a reference to the population of Indian origin, an identity marker, or a prejudiced remark. But behind the word there is a history of migration, trade, colonialism, independence, displacement, and, above all, belonging.

The question of who is Mozambican gets particularly interesting when we look at the communities of Indian origin, who have lived in the country for several generations. Are they Mozambicans? Indians? Foreigners? Or, in some cases, stateless persons? The answer cannot be found in appearance, surname, religion, or family origin alone. It is found in the country’s history and, particularly, in its nationality law.
A presence older than modern borders

The presence of people originating from the Indian subcontinent in the lands we now call Mozambique predates the country’s independence and, in many instances, predates the demarcation of the current political borders. The Indian Ocean’s trade networks connected the East African coast to South Asia long before 1975, the year Mozambique gained its independence. Over time, merchants, families, and whole communities settled in different parts of the country.

During the Portuguese colonial period, this took place within a political structure that gave people nationalities and legal statuses according to the rules of the empire. As such, “being of Indian origin” never meant automatically “being an Indian citizen.” A person can have Indian ancestry and at the same time hold Portuguese, Indian, Pakistani, or any other nationality, which could leave people in a complex bureaucratic situation. This distinction became especially important when the empire came to an end.
1975: When the question “Whose country is this?” took on a new meaning

Mozambique’s independence, made official on June 25th, 1975, did not just mean a transfer of political power. It also implied the need to define who would legally receive the new state, which was known as the New State. The Nationality Law of 1975 was key to answering that question. Among its provisions were rules that recognized as Mozambicans certain people born in the territory and resident in Mozambique at the time of independence, as well as other criteria related to birth, family links, and residence. The legislation would thus transform a heterogeneous imperial population into a national political community.

For many families of Indian origin who lived in Mozambique for decades or generations, this transformation would mean a fundamental change: no longer being legally associated with a colonial power or a foreign nationality and becoming part of the new Mozambican nation. But the experience of this transition was not the same for everybody.
When identity doesn’t fit neatly into a passport

Decolonization created situations where identity, origin, and nationality did not match. Imagine a family history across three generations: the grandparents born in India, the parents born in Mozambique during the colonial period, and the children born after independence. Which nationality should each generation have? The answer may depend on specific legal circumstances: place of birth, the parents’ nationality, residence in Mozambique at its independence, existing documentation, and any decisions to opt for or relinquish nationality.

Here, the issue of statelessness arises. A stateless person is somebody who is not considered a national by any state’s legislation. It is not an ambiguous cultural identity or feeling divided between two countries, but a legal status.

After decolonization, some people in former colonial territories, such as Angola and Mozambique, faced this problem: some were no longer recognized as nationals by the former colonial power without any other nationalities automatically being granted. This does not mean, though, that the whole Indian community in Mozambique became stateless. This generalization would be historically and legally incorrect.
“Monhé” is not a nationality

This may be where everyday language misleads us. The term “Monhé” may be used as an identity category, but it is not a legal category. Somebody called a monhé can be as Mozambican as anybody else born or naturalized in the country. They may have been born in Maputo, Nampula, Beira, or Quelimane, speak Portuguese or another Mozambican language, have had family in Mozambique for several generations, and never have lived in India. Your ancestry does not disqualify your citizenship.

Likewise, a person of Indian origin living in Mozambique can be a citizen of another country. And, in certain cases, they may have difficulties in proving or acquiring a nationality. As such, it is important to distinguish three concepts that are often confused: origin, nationality, and citizenship. A person’s origin may be Indian. Their identity can be simultaneously Mozambican and Indian. Nationality, though, is a legal relationship between an individual and a state.
The history of so-called monhés in Mozambican identity also challenges an overly simplistic view of nationality.

Mozambique has always been a space where people cross paths. Africans, Arabs, Indians, Portuguese, and other peoples participated, at different moments, in the country’s social, economic, and cultural development. The Mozambican coast, in particular, cannot be understood without movements across the Indian Ocean.

This is why it may be inappropriate to think of the Indian diaspora as forever an “outsider” population. For many of these families, Mozambique is not simply the country where they live. It is the country where they were born, where their parents were born, where their ancestors are buried, and where they built their lives. India may be their family origin. Mozambique is, for many, a homeland.

Around half a century after independence, the question of nationality continues to be more than a matter of just documents. It is a question of recognition. Who has the right to say “I am Mozambican”? Is it enough to have been born in the country? Have Mozambican parents? Have lived in the country for decades? Participate in society? Speak its languages? Share a collective memory? Or will some people continue to be seen as foreigners by many, despite legally being citizens? It is in this space between the law and general perception that many identities exist.

This evokes the concept of a “bridge” — Mozambique’s Indian-origin community historically finds itself between different spaces: Africa and Asia, family tradition and national identity, migratory memory and territorial belonging. But being between two shores does not necessarily mean not belonging to either. Sometimes it means belonging to both. And, for some, it means discovering that their family history crossed oceans long before modern passports decided which country a person belonged to.

The history of Mozambique’s monhés is thus also a history about the very meaning of being Mozambican. Not a story of people who simply “came from outside,” but a story of people who, over generations, helped build the country, while continuing to negotiate, within their families and wider society the fundamental question that follows all those who migrate: where, in the end, is home?

articles.title: Queer mediums of the cult of María Lionza are redefining the gender binary in Venezuela’s sacred mountain
articles.author: Freisy González
paras: Gender diversity, resistance and ritual cross-dressing in Venezuela's sacred cult
Originally published on Global Voices

Portrait of Wander Rodríguez, part of the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers, and the LGBTIQ+ community. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

In Venezuela, Spiritism as a religion is part of the collective imagination, of our identity; popular beliefs and ritual practices that take us back to our ancestors in colonial times. Over the years, Spiritism has evolved into a vibrant, contemporary national cult centered on the figure of María Lionza as the principal protector of waters and the charms of nature, a figure who challenges the notions of the patriarchal state and opposes monotheistic religions.

This religious system has been studied in depth by anthropologists in our country (Daisy Barreto, Angelina Pollak-Eltz, Michelle Asencio, Francisco Ferrándiz, Cesar Escalona, among others), which I had read about and found interesting at the time, but which I later witnessed for the first time in its most important sites, such as Quibayo and Sorte, in the state of Yaracuy, Venezuela.
Altar to María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

These sites are part of the Cerro María Lionza Natural Monument, popularly known as the Montaña de Sorte, and they represent the most prominent expressions of this cult nationwide, so they are visited year-round by practitioners or “caravans” (as these groups are commonly called),
But few days are as important as October 11 and 12, when thousands of people flock there to celebrate the Day of Indigenous Resistance in Venezuela.

These dates offer an opportunity for ethnographic and cultural observation, specifically how oral histories and our ethnic origins are reclaimed; including those of Indigenous peoples, some of them warriors who fought against Spanish colonization, and African populations — enslaved people and maroons — as we can understand through the figure of the Three Powers: Queen María Lionza as the central figure of the cult, the leader, accompanied by El Indio Guaicaipuro and El Negro Felipe.
Altar to Queen María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

For this celebration families gather among the trees and along the banks of the Yaracuy River, which runs through the entire mountain, setting up lavish altars to the various deities of Venezuelan spiritualism, which embody the sacred rituals characteristic of the Marialioncero cult.

The figure of María Lionza is profound, and I believe it is risky to oversimplify her, as she is regarded as a Queen, a Goddess, a mother, and a guardian, yet there are also aspects linked to her sensuality, as evidenced by the iconographic representations of her that have emerged -naked or clothed, for example-.

In this regard, I draw upon the writings of Francisco Ferrándiz and César Escalona from the perspective of Venezuelan anthropology, combining them with my own observations and field interviews, to address issues related to gender and sexual diversity that are essential to the fascinating debate within the cult on its various courts — such as the Black Court, the Viking Court, the Malandra Court, the Chamarrera Court, and the Medical Court, among others — and entities.
Detail of flowers and bottles of the Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Gender diversity, gender discrimination

The Sorte Mountain is a setting where gender stereotypes are called into question, and I believe they undermine androcentric perspectives and rigid notions of masculinity and femininity found within Christianity, since the entities pose a challenge due to their wide spectrum in terms of strength, height, voice, attire, and other details of the mediums who embody them, as well as the particular characteristics of each spirit.
Strenght between banks and Viking Court entity. Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

In his ethnographies and writings, Ferrandíz offers interesting reflections on the body and masculinity in this religion, and how male mediums (from a position of stigmatized masculinity) resisted possession by female spirits, something that did not occur as frequently among female spiritualists.
That is why my encounter in Sorte with the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers — led by Osmer Padrón and his godchildren — allowed me to also explore these aspects.
Osmer Padrón embodies the spirit of María Dolores. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

Osmer Padrón, Wander Rodríguez, and Jhonaiker Díaz are all male mediums that belong to the LGBTQ+ community, and are part of this caravan that channels female entities from the Black Court, such as María Dolores Rodríguez, Francisca Martínez, Rita Encarnación, and La Negra Tomasa; but in Osmer’s case, he also channels Mister Piter, a male entity from the Viking Court, a warrior and healer.

Wander tells me that in the LGBTQ+ spiritualist community, “there’s a lot of discrimination, both inside and outside the mountain [of Sorte], but Queen María Lionza is love and affection, and as many spiritual beings have said, we are all deeply cherished by her. We are here first and foremost to fulfill a mandate from Goddess and our Majesty María Lionza. Nothing else matters.”

Portraits of Jhonaiker Díaz (who works with the spirit of La Negra Tomasa) and José Rojas. They are part of the LGBTIQ+ community. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Regarding the practice of channeling female entities from the Black Court, Rodríguez tells me:

Most of us spiritualists in the LGBTQ+ community dress up in dresses — or find ourselves transported into that state — not because we want to… Right now, there’s a lot of talk from people saying that men who want to be women channel Black Court entities just to wear dresses, but that’s not the case. When a spiritual entity is a woman or was a woman, she always seeks to be fully covered, to cover her breasts, and why? Because she feels exposed; she feels alive. There are many spiritual entities, such as the Negra I work with — who is Rita Encarnación Martínez Chávez — as well as María Dolores Rodríguez Rodríguez, Francisca Martínez Martínez, and Negra Tomasa, who have their dresses made for them. It’s not because we want to wear dresses; if they were our own bodies, we’d walk around shirtless, but no, they always… Spirituality always seeks to feel alive; that’s why they put on their dress, their turban, and some even seek out a flower.

Dresses for female entities from the Black Court: Francisca Martínez, Francisca Palacios, María Dolores Rodríguez, Negra Tomasa and Rita Encarnación. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

There are curious details regarding what the entities ask of their “banks” —people who also care for the physical forms of the entities — such as tobacco and aguardiente; but in the case of the black women, just as they ask for their dresses, they also ask for makeup and make gestures as if looking at themselves in a mirror.

Wander tells me that, in the case of Rita Encarnación, “her favorite flower is the cayena, since it was the flower with which she learned to perform her magic, while she labels “other flowers as hypocrites, since those other flowers remain alive for many days after being plucked from nature, whereas the cayena once plucked from nature wilt immediately.”
Altar to Las Tres Potencias (The Three Powers), in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

All of this demonstrates that Venezuelan spiritism must be examined through a gender lens, from a feminist perspective, reflecting on the power dynamics established between men and women, the presence of ritual cross-dressing during trance and possession rituals, and other aspects that enrich our understanding of this important Venezuelan religion.
Wander Rodríguez enters a trance to receive the spirit of Rita Encarnación. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

articles.title: Big Tech and authoritarian states: Belarus
articles.author: Daria Dergacheva
paras: A Global Voices video podcast on the state of digital repression in Belarus
Originally published on Global Voices
Interviewer: Daria Dergacheva | Guest: Mikhail Doroshevich.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

There are more autocracies in the world in 2026 than there are democracies. Some researchers identify digital authoritarianism as the use of digital technology by regimes to surveil, repress, and manipulate domestic and foreign populations. Others argue that the same practices are also carried out by hybrid and democratic regimes. However, they can not execute them without major tech companies becoming complicit, with or without their knowledge.

Typically, when speaking about digital authoritarianism, academics and media talk about China and Russia (and occasionally Iran and Syria). However, countries such as Belarus (or Eritrea, Nicaragua, Afghanistan, Myanmar) that consistently rank as more authoritarian than China are rarely discussed.

Global Voices invited an expert on Belarusian internet, digital rights and media, Mikhail Doroshevich, on the GV video podcast “Big Tech and Authoritarian States.” We discussed why Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenka’s regime is not blocking Western social media platforms, how the internet and self-censorship are weaponized, and how platforms help the regime to spread its propaganda.
You can view and listen to the podcast in Russian on our YouTube Channel and read the translated transcript below:

Daria Dergacheva (DD): Hello, dear viewers. My name is Daria Dergacheva, and welcome to another Global Voices video podcast. Today we are discussing Big Tech and authoritarian states. Our guest is Mikhail Doroshevich, who works on digital issues in Belarus. We will speak in Russian, but an English translation and subtitles will be available. Please leave your questions in the comments and like the video.
Mikhail, welcome. Please tell us a little about yourself. This is the second Global Voices video podcast I have hosted, and today we want to focus on Belarus.

Mikhail Doroshevich (MD): I can describe myself very briefly, in one sentence: I am a researcher who has been studying the Belarusian internet for more than 30 years. A well-known political scientist once introduced me in a publication as a “veteran of the Belarusian internet.” Since then, I have jokingly used that description myself. But let us talk about something more interesting.

DD: Being a veteran of the Belarusian internet is interesting in itself! I would also like to talk about its history and what is happening now. I recently saw an article from Carnegie suggesting that the internet in Belarus remains considerably more open than in Russia. I find this paradox fascinating. How does the Belarusian regime deal with Western, Chinese, and Russian platforms?

MD: That is quite a complicated technical question. In infrastructural terms, the Belarusian internet has always been more restricted than the Russian internet. By infrastructure, I mean connectivity and connections to the global internet. Since the 1990s, Russian internet providers and mobile telecommunications companies have had their own international connections. Belarus, by contrast, has always had a vulnerable infrastructure.

International connections were controlled by state-owned companies, including the national operator. Private providers and mobile operators never had their own independent international connections. Yet today Russia restricts access to many social media services, from LinkedIn onwards, while Belarus does not impose comparable restrictions on those platforms. So Belarus historically had greater technical constraints, and shutdowns regularly accompanied political campaigns. Blocking websites and resources designated as extremist or terrorist is still widespread and ongoing. But Belarus has not followed the path Russia has taken in recent years. Their technological approaches have diverged.
DD: Do you think the platforms comply with [blocking or takedown] requests from the Belarusian state? Why is this happening?

MD: We would have to look at the platforms’ annual transparency reports. Of course the state sends requests. As far as I recall, both Meta and Google have reported receiving requests from Belarus. Whether and how they respond is another matter. That is a question for the platforms themselves. Belarus also faces restrictions imposed by technology companies. For example, some artificial intelligence services are unavailable to Belarusian users.
MD: That is OpenAI. Yes, OpenAI’s services are unavailable.

DD: In April, YouTube removed Belarusian television channels that had previously been available. Has anything changed since then, or do they remain removed? And why did the government apparently not react?

MD: The government did react. Additional channels were affected in September, with one taken down literally during a live broadcast. It is important to understand that YouTube does not simply switch a channel off without a process. It has a three-strikes system, and these channels had received strikes. They knew about them, not least because they were creating alternative channels. They tried to move their content and audiences to alternatives both in April and in September. The September ban suggests that the enforcement was connected to ownership rather than only to content. Our hypothesis about the April removals was that they were content-related: The television channels’ YouTube accounts probably violated several platform rules. Strikes can be contested after a period of time, but that involves a legal or formal procedure.
DD: So the government has not restricted YouTube in retaliation for the removal of state-media channels?

MD: No. Many other state-owned Belarusian media outlets continue to operate on YouTube and upload hundreds of videos each month. Some of the channels that were removed are trying to move their content to Rutube [a Russian video platform]. Belarus also has a domestic video platform, but neither comes close to YouTube in technical capabilities, functionality, or usage.

DD: Why do you think Lukashenko’s government has not entered into the same direct confrontation with platforms as Putin’s government? Why does it not block Western platforms? And Russian platforms such as VKontakte still work, correct?
MD: Of course they do. The authorities themselves use these platforms. That brings us back to the previous question: Why block the platforms on which they operate?
DD: Have Google or Meta services blocked state-supported media or other accounts associated with the Belarusian authorities?
MD: There have been removals following user complaints, affecting both state and independent media, but only for short periods.
DD: So there have been no major conflicts with Western, Russian, or Chinese platforms?
MD: I doubt that Chinese domestic platforms are widely used in Belarus, apart from among Chinese citizens living there. TikTok is a different case: it is not available inside China itself.
DD: Are people in Belarus punished for posts, likes, and similar activity?

MD: Yes, and it is terrible. Large numbers of people are continually subjected to repression for likes or comments. They receive actual prison sentences and fines. Unfortunately, the practice continues.
DD: Which social networks provide the information used in these cases? Are people punished for activity on Instagram, Facebook, or YouTube?
DD: Where do the authorities get information about users?
MD: They use, for example, Russian tools for social profiling.
DD: So you believe this is external monitoring?

MD: I do not think the platforms are doing the monitoring. The authorities monitor users themselves, identify them, and punish them. People are also punished for subscriptions to channels discovered during searches of their devices.
DD: For example, subscribing to NEXTA [a progressive, exiled Russian-language media site] could lead to punishment?
DD: What sort of sentences do people receive?
MD: They can be enormous and appalling. Even a minimum sentence would be a deeply troubling precedent in itself.
DD: So people practice self-censorship: they avoid liking, reposting, or writing things?

MD: Of course. It is a matter of personal safety and, unfortunately, part of everyday life in Belarus. But it is important to understand that avoiding these activities does not necessarily make people safer. Nor does it improve national security. What increases is repression. The costs of these measures are unjustifiable: they do not make life in Belarus safer or more peaceful.

If there were some sort of social contract in which restrictions led to fewer crimes or greater security, that would at least be an argument. But that is not what happens. People face severe financial penalties and restrictions for likes and reposts. You know how these platforms work: someone can accidentally like something while scrolling. People of all ages are affected, from young people to the elderly. Older users may be especially vulnerable to accidental interactions. And if we look at online fraud and other cybercrime, even official statistics show that these problems are not decreasing.

Restricting access to information resources does not reduce cybercrime. Preventive measures, media literacy, and education would do much more to protect people from criminals. Those would be more important and meaningful goals.
DD: As far as I know, Russia actively uses social media platforms, including Western ones, to spread disinformation or propaganda, whichever term you prefer. Does Belarus do the same?
MD: If Belarusian state actors are active on these platforms, then, as you can imagine, they do.
DD: Do you mean through official accounts, or also through trolls?

MD: There is an important distinction here. State news agencies and state-owned media generally observe certain boundaries in their written website publications, even when they present events in a particular way. You do not usually see direct hate speech or doxxing in those articles.

Unfortunately, television material is different. The proportion of such content is much higher in videos than in official written publications. So the same outlet might have a relatively restrained website, with its own preferred formulations, while its YouTube channel contains doxxing, hate speech, and other unacceptable material.
Then there is a third layer: individual, highly toxic channels, which are not meaningfully restricted and can behave much more aggressively.
DD: Do you mean individual propagandists, like those in Russia? Are they mostly funded by the state?

MD: They presumably receive their salaries from their state-owned employers. Whether they make these videos during working hours is something we do not know. But they certainly do not hold back in their language.
DD: What technologies are used to monitor people, including facial recognition and internet surveillance? Are they Western, Chinese, Russian, or domestically developed?

MD: I cannot tell you the exact manufacturers or versions of the software being used. More technically informed specialists would need to answer that. But we regularly see cases in which software developed in democratic countries, not only authoritarian ones, ends up being used in such systems. Unfortunately, when funding is available, companies enter tenders, and the products that meet the purchaser’s requirements are selected and deployed.
DD: Could this be investigated through publicly available procurement information?

MD: I do not follow Belarusian procurement tenders for facial recognition or monitoring systems. That is a separate specialization. There is also a conceptual problem: If a system uses TCP/IP, does that make it Western, Chinese, or Russian technology? TCP/IP itself was not developed in Russia or China.
DD: I know, for example, that many cameras in Moscow are Chinese, and Huawei servers are widely used in some parts of the infrastructure.
MD: That distinction is tricky. Look at where your phone was manufactured. Even if its brand is not associated with China, the device may have been made there.
DD: Of course. In the European Union, there are restrictions on using equipment from certain Chinese companies. I do not know the precise situation in the United States or Canada.

MD: Yes, Belarusian mobile operators use such equipment, and that is a significant issue. There is a similar problem with access to AI models. When Belarusians cannot use certain services, they may turn to Chinese or Russian models, which are censored and limited in various ways. One positive exception is Google’s Gemini, which is available in Belarus.
DD: What about Llama? It is open source.

MD: Yes, but there are questions about its capabilities. We return again to education and skills. People need to know how to use and maintain these models. Open source does not mean free to operate. Running and maintaining a model can be more expensive than simply using a proprietary service.
DD: Remind me why OpenAI and Anthropic do not operate in Belarus. Is it a matter of company policy?

MD: Possibly. There are also sanctions. TikTok, for instance, has imposed restrictions on its Russian operations since 2022, and Belarusian accounts have been used to get around those restrictions. Other social networks do not impose the same restrictions on Russian users as TikTok does.

DD: I have two more questions. Belarus used to have a rapidly developing IT sector, and the government supported some of that growth. What is happening now? Are companies still developing technology, or has everyone left? Does Belarus have its own data centers? Are Russian or Western data centers used? Can Belarusian citizens’ data be stored abroad? And are there domestic AI developments, perhaps based on open-source models?

MD: Let me start at the end. Yes, there is development based on open-source models. As for data storage, the relevant data must be kept in data centers certified by the Operational and Analytical Center, which means in Belarus. The country certainly has its own data centers.
DD: And how is the IT sector doing overall?

MD: It is developing. With the rise of AI, the entire sector worldwide is undergoing a transformation. As for companies that remain in Belarus, their customers are predominantly in the Russian Federation.
DD: Does that mean they also work for Russian military organizations?

MD: We cannot know that without looking at particular companies. It is more a question for specialists familiar with Russia’s infrastructure. Hypothetically, the Russian military might itself face restrictions on contracting developers even from countries such as Kazakhstan, Belarus, or other former Soviet states. So I would not assume that the Russian army uses Belarusian developments. But customers are not only military organizations. And many companies have offices in several countries while still employing hundreds or thousands of people in Belarus. They may be global companies with substantial Belarusian operations.

DD: Thank you very much. We will publish an English transcript of this interview on our website, and the video will be available on YouTube. Thank you again for your time. I hope we will see each other again.
MD: Thank you for your work. It is genuinely impressive. I enjoy reading the material Global Voices produces; it is very interesting.

articles.title: In Brazil’s elections, big techs’ transparency and cooperation policies translate as governance washing, according to this expert
articles.author: Fernanda Canofre
paras: Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University NetLab has been following closely how this election unfolds on social media
Originally published on Global Voices
Art by Global Voices, created in Canva Pro.

Amid a series of corruption scandals, the 2026 general election in Brazil is also flooded with headlines about social media companies’ role in the campaign. Users supporting the candidacy of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the incumbent center-left candidate running for re-election, have been reporting a sudden drop in their Instagram Stories views when posting about politics. They say that Meta AI refused to generate images featuring Lula’s name and party number, while delivering the same request for Flávio Bolsonaro, his far-right opponent and the son of the imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro.

On October 16, Meta admitted technical problems on its platforms which affected how pro-Lula content was delivered to users. As reported by the Associated Press, despite acknowledging “global technical glitches, strict anti-fraud measures, and regulatory compliance rather than targeted suppression,” the company that owns Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook denied any political bias.

Lula filed a complaint against Meta accusing the company of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favor Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election, with a judge from the country’s top electoral court ruling that Meta must adopt measures to ensure equal treatment.

With an estimated population of 214 million, Brazil is an important market for social media platforms. It ranks as the second country by number of WhatsApp users and saw the internet become a key component of Jair Bolsonaro’s ascent around 10 years ago.

To understand the current election scenario, Global Voices spoke to Nicole Sanchotene, project coordinator at NetLab, a research laboratory at Rio de Janeiro’s Federal University (UFRJ) that has been publishing reports on the impact of big tech on the electoral campaign. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
Global Voices: What have you identified in NetLab’s recent reports about the elections?

Nicole Sanchotene: É muito difícil avaliar o impacto e os possíveis efeitos para a disputa eleitoral e para a percepção das pessoas. O problema central que a gente tem apontado é sobre transparência, uma certa normalização de possíveis ilícitos eleitorais, pontos que são consenso na resolução do TSE (Tribunal Superior Eleitoral) e não estamos vendo cumprimento pleno das plataformas. O Kwai, que é uma plataforma com ampla adesão no Brasil, tem mais de 60 milhões de usuários, é bastante usado pelas classes C e D, fez uma parceria com o TSE e não está adequado. Não atende a requisitos básicos, a biblioteca de anúncios político-eleitorais tem falhas no tipo de dado que entrega. A gente tem chamado essas práticas de transparência de fachada. Cada uma das plataformas tem um problema específico. Seja por dados incompletos, seja pela veiculação ou recomendação de conteúdo que não deveria ser recomendado. O que a gente vê é que elas não estão respeitando plenamente o que é exigido pelas normas brasileiras para garantir um mínimo de condições de igualdade para os candidatos, condições que permitam um ambiente de informação, de propaganda, seguro para os usuários e para a disputa eleitoral.

Nicole Sanchotene: It’s hard to evaluate the impact and possible effects on the running and on people’s perception. The central issue that we’ve been pointing to is transparency, a certain normalization of possible illicit electoral practices, issues that were agreed upon in the TSE [Superior Electoral Court, Brazil's top electoral court] resolution, and we are not seeing the platforms comply fully. Kwai, a platform with widespread adoption in Brazil, with over 60 million users and largely used by “C and D classes” [lower income groups and the basis of the socio-economic pyramid], partnered with the electoral court, and it’s not suitable yet. It doesn't meet basic requirements; their library for political-electoral ads has flaws in the data delivered. We have been calling this a ‘façade of transparency.’ Each platform has a specific issue. Incomplete data, the publishing or recommendation of content that shouldn't be recommended. What we are seeing is that they are not fully abiding by Brazilian norms to guarantee minimum conditions of equality for the candidates, nor conditions that allow an information and publicty environment safe for users and the electoral running itself.
GV: How important are such platforms in Brazilians’ daily lives?

NS: Tem um relatório da Reuters que mostra como as pessoas se informam cada vez mais pelas redes sociais, por plataformas como YouTube, Instagram. O WhatsApp é uma fonte onde as pessoas recebem informações de pessoas próximas, e elas tendem a confiar em pessoas próximas. O Brasil é um dos grandes mercados do WhatsApp, diversas camadas das nossas interações sociais, profissionais passam por ali. A gente não tem condições de falar de disputa eleitoral sem passar pelas redes sociais e sem passar especificamente pelas plataformas da Meta.

NS: There is a Reuters report that shows how people are getting information more and more from social media, through platforms such as YouTube and Instagram. WhatsApp is a source through which they get information from those who are closer to them, which they tend to trust more. Brazil is a big market for WhatsApp; several layers of our social and professional interactions pass through it. We cannot discuss the electoral dispute without going through social media, especially Meta’s platforms.

GV: People have claimed they noticed a sudden drop in their Instagram stories views after posting about politics, especially if they are leftists. Leandro Demori, a journalist, published screenshots showing his stories fell from an average of one million or 400,000 views to 9,000. Have you been reporting on that?

NS: Não fizemos nenhuma análise em relação a isso. Mas acho que essa discussão tem a ver com a questão da transparência. Não é exclusivo da Meta. Essas plataformas tomam decisões – quanto um anúncio vai custar, que tipo de conteúdo vai aparecer ou não para um determinado usuário, decisões de moderação – em uma grande caixa-preta. Ninguém sabe como elas são tomadas, não existem mecanismos para fiscalizar. Um argumento que a gente costuma ver com muita frequência é plataformas falando que são intermediárias, empresas de tecnologia, e estão à disposição para serem usadas por quem quiser. E a gente sabe que não é assim. Elas usam os dados dos usuários para recomendar conteúdo e direcionar anúncios, seguindo uma série de decisões editoriais, como uma curadoria, sem possibilidade de escrutínio. A venda de anúncios para anunciantes, por exemplo, é um sistema completamente opaco. O anunciante compra o anúncio, existe uma promessa de entrega do conteúdo ao usuário, mas ele não sabe efetivamente se esse conteúdo está sendo entregue. E da mesma maneira, nós pesquisadores, jornalistas, o poder público, não temos como saber como essa distribuição de conteúdo é feita. Os algoritmos são uma grande caixa-preta. A gente consegue fazer alguns testes, mas sempre no nível experimental, porque não existe uma ferramenta que permita isso. Em condições normais, isso já é muito sério, porque a plataforma decide o fluxo de informações numa sociedade, mas quando se aplica a uma disputa eleitoral, tudo fica ainda mais sério. Pode ser que os candidatos estejam concorrendo em condições que não são iguais.

NS: We haven’t analyzed this. But I think it has to do with transparency. It’s not exclusive to Meta. These platforms make decisions — how much an ad is going to cost, what kind of ad will show up or not to a certain user, moderation decisions — in a big black box (flight recorder). No one knows how they are made; there are no mechanisms to oversee it. An argument we used to hear often is that companies themselves say they are intermediaries, tech companies, available to whoever wants to use them. And we know is not the way it is.
